h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in New Hampshire
intro:
New Hampshire draws investors for reasons that have little to do with buildings: no state tax on wage income, no general sales tax and a short drive from Boston. The buildings, though, decide whether a deal works. The state's rental housing is concentrated in old mill cities along the Merrimack and the Cocheco, where wood tenements and three-deckers built for textile and shoe workers now need roofs, heat, porches and lead work, often all at once.

Genstone Construction renovates investor property in New Hampshire, with a dedicated page for Manchester. We will look at a Granite State property before you buy it, price the likely repairs and check your target value, free of charge. Once you own the property, you receive an itemized scope and draw schedule, a field manager running vetted, licensed local trades and permit and inspection handling with the town or city. Nothing is due upfront; draws follow completed work, and the final payment comes after you approve the job. That structure matters in a state that does not license general contractors, because accountability has to come from the process rather than a state credential.

sections.body:
New Hampshire's investor housing is heaviest in the mill cities. Manchester grew around the Amoskeag Millyard and still has brick corporation housing near the river, plus West Side streets lined with wood three-deckers, duplexes and three- and four-story tenement blocks, many with flat roofs. Nashua, Concord, Dover, Rochester, Somersworth and Laconia have similar, smaller concentrations of late nineteenth and early twentieth-century multifamily housing near their former mills.

Around those cities, the stock turns suburban. Bedford, Londonderry, Hooksett and Merrimack have post-war Capes and ranches and later Colonials and split-levels. The Seacoast, led by Portsmouth, has some of the oldest housing in the country alongside high-priced newer construction. The Lakes Region and the White Mountains have seasonal cottages, camps and condos, many on private wells and septic systems.

Throughout the older stock, expect lead paint, balloon framing, knob-and-tube or early wiring, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains. Oil heat remains common, often through a single boiler in multifamily buildings. Foundations range from granite block and fieldstone to poured concrete, and ledge is frequent enough to complicate excavation. New Hampshire's granite bedrock also makes radon common in basements, and private wells can carry arsenic or radon in the water, so testing belongs in due diligence.

The Merrimack Valley, running from Nashua through Manchester to Concord, holds most of the state's rental housing and investor activity. Manchester's West Side, inner East Side and neighborhoods like Rimmon Heights, Bakersville and Hallsville are dominated by multifamily buildings suited to buy-and-hold and BRRRR plans, supported by healthcare, college, airport and technology employment and by households moving north from Massachusetts. Nashua has similar dynamics closer to the border. Concord, the state capital, adds government employment.

Flips perform strongest where owner-occupants dominate: Manchester's North End and South End, suburban towns around the cities and parts of the Seacoast. Buyers in these markets often use FHA, New Hampshire Housing or conventional loans, so renovations must satisfy appraisals and lender condition standards.

The Seacoast is a higher-priced market with strong demand from both year-round residents and buyers relocating from greater Boston. The Lakes Region and mountain towns offer seasonal and short-term rental opportunities, with renovations shaped by septic capacity, well water and access. The Dover-Rochester area offers mill-era multifamily housing at lower prices than Portsmouth.

Across the state, low inventory has supported rents and resale prices, but aging buildings and a short exterior building season make accurate repair estimates and realistic schedules essential.

sections.h2: Permits and licensing in New Hampshire
sections.body:
New Hampshire adopts a state building code and state fire code based on the International Codes, and municipalities enforce them locally. Larger cities like Manchester, Nashua and Concord have full building departments; Manchester's Building Regulations division within Planning and Community Development is one example. Some smaller towns have more limited local enforcement, so it is important to confirm what each town requires before starting work.

The licensing picture is different from Massachusetts and Connecticut. New Hampshire does not license general contractors, and there is no statewide home improvement registration. Electricians and plumbers must hold state licenses, and fuel gas and oil burner work also require licensed technicians. Because anyone can operate as a general contractor, vetting insurance, references and track record is especially important.

Older rentals carry lead obligations. With broader childhood blood-lead screening now in place, more New Hampshire rentals are being tied to lead cases, and the state can then require hazard reduction. Federal lead-safe work rules govern any paint disturbance in those older buildings.

Properties on private septic systems fall under state Department of Environmental Services rules, and work affecting septic capacity, such as adding bedrooms, may require state approval. Shoreland protection rules apply near lakes and rivers.

New Hampshire winters are long and cold, and they get colder and snowier the farther north and higher you go. Even in Manchester and Nashua, temperatures fall well below coastal Massachusetts, and frost drives deep into the ground. Porch and addition footings must sit below frost depth, and anything set shallow will heave.

Snow load is a real structural concern on older roofs, particularly the flat roofs on Manchester's tenement blocks and lightly framed roofs on camps and older farmhouses. Ice dams are common wherever attic insulation is poor. The Seacoast sees less snow than the interior but more exposure to nor'easters and salt air.

The exterior building season runs roughly from late spring into fall. April's mud season can bog down an excavator, delay septic repairs and turn a rural driveway impassable. Roofing, siding, painting, porch reconstruction and masonry are ideally scheduled in the warmer months, and concrete and mortar need protection when temperatures fall.

Inside, crews can keep working through January, provided a vacant building has heat or has been properly drained. Frozen and burst pipes are among the most expensive problems in vacant New Hampshire property. Spring snowmelt and heavy rains can also bring river flooding in low-lying areas along the Merrimack and its tributaries.

faqs.q: Where does Genstone work in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: We have a dedicated page for Manchester, and our network of vetted, licensed contractors also serves nearby communities including Bedford, Goffstown, Hooksett, Londonderry, Merrimack and the Nashua area. Genstone runs New Hampshire jobs from its Romeoville, Illinois headquarters through local licensed trades, with a field manager assigned to each property to keep the schedule, inspections and records. Concord, Dover and the Seacoast can be reached through the same network when a project calls for it.

faqs.q: Why is contractor vetting so important in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: Because the state does not license general contractors, a company can take on renovation work without any state credential. Electrical, plumbing and fuel work still require licensed tradespeople, but the general contractor running the job does not. Genstone vets the local contractors in our network for required licenses, insurance and track record, and our field managers oversee the work so standards stay consistent across projects.

faqs.q: Should investors test for radon and arsenic?
faqs.a: Yes. New Hampshire's granite bedrock makes radon common in basements, and private wells can contain arsenic or radon in the water. Lenders, buyers and tenants increasingly ask for test results. If testing shows a problem, radon mitigation and water treatment systems are usually manageable costs, especially when installed during a renovation rather than after finishes are complete. We can coordinate testing as part of the pre-offer review.

faqs.q: Do you handle FHA 203(k) projects in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: Yes. Our FHA 203(k) contractor certification applies in New Hampshire as everywhere we work. Owner-occupied two- to four-unit buildings in Manchester and other mill cities, along with older single-family homes needing systems and energy upgrades, are strong candidates. We prepare lender-ready bids, coordinate with HUD consultants and plan the work around draw inspections and New Hampshire's short exterior building season. Agents often call us before writing the offer.
